headline_fact: Look at the diagonal weave before judging denim by its colour.
summary: Learn to recognise denim, understand its construction and consider how different versions behave.
did_you_know: A fabric name and a fibre name describe different things.
core_mechanics: A twill weave creates diagonal lines; the yarns and finishing affect how the fabric feels.
why_it_matters: Recognising construction helps you ask better questions about a garment.

in_depth_breakdown.real_world_application: A trolley carrying more mass needs more net force to achieve the same acceleration.

learning_takeaways: Look for construction details, not colour alone.
A fibre and a fabric are different things.

fashion_lesson.hook: Look at the diagonal weave before judging denim by its colour.
fashion_lesson.question: What makes denim more than a blue fabric?
fashion_lesson.learning_goal: Recognise a few visible details, then connect the weave and materials with everyday use.

introduction.explanation: Denim is a fabric rather than a fibre. A familiar example uses a twill weave with differently coloured yarns. Looking at the face, reverse and diagonal lines helps explain the appearance of the material.
introduction.why_it_matters: Two garments can share a colour while using very different fabrics. Recognising the structure gives you a better starting point than the colour alone.

recognition_guide.where_to_look: Look closely at an unobstructed area of the fabric. Follow the small repeating lines across its face.
recognition_guide.why_it_matters: The diagonal pattern helps you recognise a twill construction.
recognition_guide.comparison: A plain weave has a different interlacing pattern; blue colour alone does not identify denim.

recognition_guide.feature: A difference between face and reverse
recognition_guide.where_to_look: Compare the outer face with the inside of a cuff or an unfinished sample.
recognition_guide.why_it_matters: Different yarns can be more visible on each face. This helps explain why the inside can look lighter.

recognition_guide.where_to_look: Examine the texture and the material information on the actual item.
recognition_guide.why_it_matters: Cotton is a fibre; denim names a fabric. Some versions include other fibres that change their behaviour.

origin_and_context.explanation: Denim has a history of workwear and later fashion use. Its materials, production methods and meanings change across places and periods.
origin_and_context.uncertainty: Names and origin stories can be more complicated than a single place or invention date.
origin_and_context.deeper_history: A full history can follow the cloth, its production and the garments made from it separately. The material and the clothing do not have identical histories.

materials.name: Cotton
materials.role: Cotton can supply the yarns used to weave the cloth.
materials.tradeoffs: The fibre content alone does not tell you the thickness, finishing or comfort of the final item.

materials.name: Denim cloth
materials.role: The woven structure brings yarns together into the fabric used for garments.
materials.tradeoffs: Different weights and finishes can make denim feel quite different. A fabric name is not a universal performance guarantee.

construction.title: The twill structure
construction.explanation: A repeating interlacing pattern produces the small diagonal lines. The yarns and finishing also affect the surface, so the weave is one part of the explanation.
construction.visible_effect: Look for a diagonal repeat rather than treating every blue fabric as denim.

wearing_properties.explanation: A heavier sample may feel more substantial, while a lighter sample can move more freely.
wearing_properties.depends_on: The actual weight, fibre blend, finishing and garment cut all matter.

wearing_properties.explanation: Some versions feel firm and others feel soft. Feel the actual item rather than relying on its colour.
wearing_properties.depends_on: The yarns, weave and treatments affect the surface.

practical_guide.introduction: Connect the fabric with the way the finished item is used.
use_examples: Notice denim in jeans, jackets and other garments. Compare the fabrics instead of assuming they are identical.
fit_and_movement: Check whether the actual garment lets you sit, reach and move comfortably.
climate_considerations: Consider fabric weight and garment coverage for the conditions in which you plan to wear it.

care.reason: The maker can specify care for the actual fabric, finish and construction.
care.limits: Do not apply one washing rule to every denim blend or finish.

care.reason: Some dyed fabrics can transfer colour under certain conditions.
care.limits: Check the maker’s guidance; this example does not establish colourfastness.

care.reason: A finish or added component may need a different approach.
care.limits: Ask the maker when the label does not explain how to care for the item.

variations.name: Lighter and heavier versions
variations.difference: Different weights can suit different constructions. Weight alone does not determine quality.

misconceptions.correction: Colour is not enough to identify a fabric.
misconceptions.explanation: Look at the weave and the material information on the actual item.

takeaways: Look for construction details, not colour alone.
A fibre and a fabric are different things.
